gist: A 64-bit counter that never collides across data centers. Ten million IDs per second, roughly time ordered, answered locally in under a millisecond with no network round trip. The whole design is a bit budget: how to split 64 bits between time, machine, and sequence.

1: About 10 million IDs per second at peak across all services
IDs are unique across data centers and never reused
IDs are roughly time ordered so a one hour range scan reads few pages
A strong candidate asks for rate, ordering strength, and the bit budget instead of inventing them.
2: Two shapes: a central issuing service, or local generation from a machine id plus time
A central service needs a network round trip per ID; the requirement forbids that
Sketch the local shape: machine id assigned once, timestamp and sequence fill the rest
A strong candidate rejects the central issuer on the round trip requirement alone.
3: 64 bits split like: 41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits of machine, 12 bits of sequence
41 bits of milliseconds covers about 70 years; 12 bits of sequence gives 4096 IDs per millisecond per machine, about 4 million per second
Three machines cover the 10 million per second peak; 1024 machine ids give huge headroom
Rough ordering falls out of the timestamp bits; only IDs within one millisecond on one machine need the sequence
A strong candidate does the bit arithmetic out loud and checks the peak against it.
4: The bottleneck is the bit budget, not throughput: 4096 IDs per millisecond per machine bounds burst on one node
Burst beyond 4096 per millisecond spills to another machine or waits for the next millisecond
Machine id assignment happens once at boot through coordination, not per ID
A local call answers in under 1 ms because no network ride sits in the path
A strong candidate knows the sequence limit and where overflow goes.
5: A clock that steps back up to 5 seconds must not reuse sequence space: wait out the drift or bump a generation
Time ordering survives data center boundaries because timestamps compare across sites
Range scans on a one hour window read a narrow time band of the index
A strong candidate explains what breaks if the clock lies, and bounds it.

anchors.1: Hearing the rate: the candidate states 10 million IDs per second at peak
anchors.2: Hearing the uniqueness domain: the candidate guarantees uniqueness across data centers with no reuse ever
anchors.3: Hearing the order: the candidate makes IDs roughly time ordered so one hour scans read few pages
anchors.4: Hearing the locality: the candidate generates locally with no network round trip per ID, under 1 ms
anchors.5: Hearing the budget: the candidate fits every ID in 64 bits and splits time, machine, and sequence
anchors.6: Hearing the clock: the candidate tolerates a 5 second backward step without reusing IDs

probes.q: IDs must never be reused. What does 'never' cost you when a machine restarts mid-millisecond?
Why not a database that hands out IDs? What does the requirement forbid?
Split 64 bits your way. How many years does your timestamp last, and how many IDs per second can one machine emit?
One machine gets a burst of 10 thousand ID requests in one millisecond. What exactly happens?
The clock on one node jumps back 5 seconds. Walk me through the IDs it emits next.
Your service stores IDs in a database index. Why does rough time order matter for a one hour range scan?
